content.title: What are peptides?
content.text: The longevity industry loves a buzzword, and the latest is ‘peptide’. Billed as the solution to everything from a wonky metabolism to age-related decline in muscle repair, these things are all over our feeds right now. You’ll find pills, powders, creams and sprays in this corner of the internet, but the majority of gym bros chatting about peptides online are referencing the injectable stuff. Put the term into TikTok, and you’ll be met with a quarter of a million videos and counting, with titles like ‘Three peptides to live to 100’, ‘Peptides NOT steroids’ and ‘POV you got $2k+ worth of peptides for $200 on grey market’.Questionable grammar aside, videos like these raise larger questions. Yes, peptides are everywhere, but do they actually work, and are they even safe? Forget the online influencers; here, we consulted bona fide healthcare professionals for their considered views on the latest trend. And while some are cautiously optimistic, their assessment comes with heavy caveats…Sorry, what exactly are peptides?Peptides are the strings of amino acids that form the building blocks of proteins. The body produces peptides continuously, and these molecules help cells communicate and respond to change. “This signalling is essential for tissues with high turnover, including the skin,” says Dr Kevita Bains, a consultant at the Revive Clinic in London. “More broadly, peptides influence inflammation, wound healing, immune response and metabolic regulation across the body.”Crucially, these communication pathways slow with age, which is why it can take us longer to recover or lose weight as we get older. Peptide treatments are designed to keep all of this ticking over like it did before we started complaining about back pain and receding hairlines.“The most famous peptide treatment at the moment is the GLP-1 agonist,” adds Dr Kaywaan Khan, GP and founder of Hannah London Clinic. That’s your Wegovy and other weight loss drugs. But recently, other peptides, like Teriparatide, Linaclotide, and Ziconotide, are getting buzz online for their claims to treat everything from hormone regulation and inflammation to energy levels and tissue repair. The deeply problematic manosphere bro Clavicular, for example, uses a peptide called Melanotan II to get more tanned skin, since it can trigger hyperpigmentation. Across TikTok, bodybuilding bros often show off their toned abs and credit a “stack” of peptides (most commonly, Ipamorelin and CJC1295) in the caption… with a private discount code, of course.Why is everyone talking about them right now?Rick Brennan, a former AFL player turned high-performance coach, thinks our obsession with optimising everything from sleep to skin is partly to blame, with peptides being seen as a universal health panacea for the time-poor among us. “The majority of interest I see is from my corporate clients: busy CEOs, professional athletes, actors and very successful professional people looking for a better version of themselves," he says.But while most of the online crowd is only now catching on, peptides aren’t anything new. “Peptide-based treatments have been used in medicine for decades, but public awareness has really surged with the rise of GLP-1 medications, with platforms like TikTok making complex medical concepts feel more accessible,” Kahn says, adding that, with most of us downing various supplements daily, peptide injections have retained an attractive air of exclusivity as “the next-level upgrade”.Do they actually work?With the peptide industry estimated to be worth $81.5 billion (£60bn) by 2034, this is quite literally the multi-billion dollar question. But answers about efficacy aren't necessarily clear-cut.“The evidence for peptides varies depending on which peptide you're looking at and what you're hoping to achieve,” says Bains. The benefits of GLP-1s are well-documented, with a 2024 study in the journal Cell Metabolism finding that GLP-1 receptor activation not only reduces weight but also helps fight inflammation in the body.Skincare is its own peptide rodeo. There is some limited data to back up certain anti-ageing claims, but not enough to prove anything conclusive.On the bodybuilding front, Khan says fitness communities are piling on because certain peptides have been shown to rapidly stimulate the release of growth hormone and influence muscle growth, fat loss, and exercise recovery. Scientists know that naturally occurring peptides can do this. But evidence supporting the efficiency and safety of fancy, re-packaged treatments online is next to non-existent.
